summary.text: The identity matrix is a square matrix with ones on the main diagonal and zeros everywhere else.
Multiplying by it is analogous to multiplying by the number 1, and as a geometric transformation it leaves every object unchanged.
It is its own inverse, and two square matrices multiply to give it exactly when each is the inverse of the other.

facts.label: Shape
facts.value: Square, with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere

facts.label: Role
facts.value: Plays the part of the number 1 in multiplication

facts.label: Own inverse
facts.value: It is involutory: equal to its own inverse

facts.label: Test for inverses
facts.value: Two square matrices have it as product exactly when inverses

facts.label: Principal square root
facts.value: Its principal square root is itself

items.prompt: Which pattern describes the identity matrix?

options.label: Every entry equal to one
Ones along the main diagonal, zeros elsewhere
Zeros along the main diagonal, ones elsewhere
Ones in the first row, zeros elsewhere

items.explain: It is a square matrix with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere.

items.prompt: A graphics program applies a transformation whose matrix is the identity matrix. What happens to the shape on screen?

options.label: It is rotated a quarter turn
It is flipped over
It shrinks to a single point
It stays exactly as it was

items.explain: When the identity matrix represents a geometric transformation, the object remains unchanged.

items.prompt: Multiplying by the identity matrix is like which everyday arithmetic move?

options.label: Multiplying a number by 1
Multiplying a number by 0
Adding 1 to a number
Squaring a number

items.explain: It is analogous to multiplying by the number 1, which leaves things as they were.

items.prompt: Some matrices are equal to their own inverse. Which of these is such a matrix?

options.label: A square matrix filled entirely with zeros
A square matrix filled entirely with ones
The square matrix with ones down the diagonal
A square matrix with one single nonzero entry

items.explain: The identity matrix is invertible and is an involutory matrix, equal to its own inverse.

items.prompt: Two square matrices are multiplied together and the result is the identity matrix. What does this tell you about them?

options.label: Both of them must be the identity matrix
Each one is the inverse of the other
They must be equal to each other
One of them must be filled with zeros

items.explain: Two square matrices have the identity matrix as their product exactly when they are inverses of each other.

items.prompt: For an identity matrix with at least two rows, how many symmetric matrices square to it?

options.label: Exactly one, the identity itself
Exactly two, the identity and its negative
None, because it has no square root
Infinitely many

items.explain: Every identity matrix with at least two rows and columns has an infinitude of symmetric square roots, although its principal square root is itself.
